etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English ferful, fervol, equivalent to fear +‎ -ful.

quote.citation: c. 1588–1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Lamentable Tragedy of Titus Andronicus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene ii]:
quote.text: Sirs, stop their mouths, let them not speak to me,But let them hear what fearful words I utter.

quote.citation: 1981, William Irwin Thompson, The Time Falling Bodies Take to Light: Mythology, Sexuality and the Origins of Culture, London: Rider/Hutchinson & Co., page 184:
quote.text: In the later Hebrew midrash Lilith is presented as the woman who knows how to recite the fearful name of God to work calamity; that this little girl cries out the fearful name of the sun god and thereby causes an earthquake would indicate that this girl is linked in the structure of the myth with Lilith.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book III, Canto IV”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: Those two great champions did attonce pursew / The fearefull damzell with incessant payns  […]

quote.citation: 2009, Juliette Shapiro, Mr. Darcy's Decision: A Sequel to Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice:
quote.text: “He is fearful handsome, as you know,” she said remorsefully, “you cannot imagine, Georgiana, the joy when I first fell in love with him.”

quote.citation: 2014, Diana Wynne Jones, The Chrestomanci series:
quote.text: “It's a fearful strong charm needs dragon's blood,” he said plaintively.

quote.text: His Dardanelles expedition gave the Turk a fearful long start.
